Some Linux distros are steering clear of AI. China’s openKylin embraces AI.

Prague — Many Linux distros such as Gentoo , Void Linux , and System76’s COSMIC desktop hate AI. Linus Torvalds, on the other hand, said at Open Source Summit Europe , “I actually really like using AI.” Then, there’s China’s openKylin community-developed Linux distribution, which makes no bones about it. They’re all about putting AI front and center.

As openKylin executive director Liu Min explained in her keynote at Open Source Summit Europe, the operating system is moving beyond managing computing resources to organizing AI capabilities and, ultimately, users’ intent through its KylinBot AI agent framework.

With KylinBot, instead of the usual hands-on desktop experience, it’s all about intent management: understanding what a user wants, coordinating models, data, tools, and devices, and executing the resulting tasks within defined permissions.

The shift is from resource management to capability management, but Liu observed: “Resource management remains the foundation.” In short, openKylin 3.0 , its latest release, attempts to build AI into the desktop’s operating architecture rather than merely bundling a chatbot with a Linux distribution.

Specifically, openKylin says KylinBot can understand user requests by voice and chat, retain context across interactions, and use system capabilities to help you do work. By integrating Kylin-CUA, an automation tool, KylinBot can access capabilities such as system settings and device management, moving AI beyond answering questions toward executing tasks.

What this looks like in practice is that KylinBot provides the agent framework, while Xiao K supplies an assistant interface built on top of it. Available system skills cover input devices, display settings, networking, Bluetooth peripherals, power management, and other desktop controls. For example, you can request a different network connection, disable Bluetooth, or change a keyboard layout by talking or chatting with KylinBot, without touching the usual settings controls.

The project also integrates Kylin-CUA. This computer-use automation tool extends agent access to system settings and device-management functions. It also supports third-party agent tools, such as OpenClaw and WorkBuddy .

This integration is central to openKylin 3.0, the latest release. In it, the Linux desktop becomes something an agent can operate, not simply somewhere an agent’s chat window runs.

Liu’s keynote placed these features in a layered architecture. Familiar Linux, drivers, and hardware resources remain the foundation. Above them sit local inference capabilities and shared AI runtime services, followed by agents that plan tasks and coordinate tools. Computer-use automation extends those agents’ reach to traditional graphical applications.

Under the hood, openKylin includes conventional Linux-platform upgrades alongside its AI work. For example, openKylin 3.0 uses Linux 7.0, optimizes more than 180 core components, improves RISC-V support, and expands Rust’s use in its Linux system tools.

Liu added that the project includes intelligent search that locates information by content and description. This reduces reliance on knowing a file’s location and on intelligent workspaces by collecting relevant files around a task. These were presented as part of the project’s exploration of how AI changes desktop interaction, rather than as independently demonstrated results.

OpenKylin is still a work in progress. Liu explained, “Open source makes AI capability accessible, but accessibility is only the beginning,” Making it useful, she added, requires system engineering: understanding how models run, connect to data and applications, and work across different hardware environments.

This Chinese open-source Linux distribution primarily focuses on desktop computing. It serves as a technical upstream for the commercial Kylin operating system.

OpenKylin is also exploring uses beyond the traditional desktop. These include smart devices, industrial automation, robotics, high-performance computing, and cloud environments. Those are development directions. It doesn’t yet provide an equally mature platform for every workload.

Another concern its developers are aware of is its security. After all, an AI agent that can change settings and operate applications raises numerous concerns. Liu identified agent security and governance as a continuing priority, including who authorizes actions, which actions are permitted, and how a human can intervene.

As openKylin Technical Committee chair Wu Qingbo added, openKylin is exploiting a fundamental architectural change. “The shift from ‘AI as an application’ to ‘AI as an operating system’ is not simply a feature upgrade, but a transformation of the underlying architecture.” Looking ahead, he expects its open ecosystem and architecture will enable developers to extend intelligent capabilities “more transparently and securely” while accommodating more hardware, such as RISC-V .

Or, as Liu’s closing statement put it: “Open source brings innovation together. Operating systems make intelligence usable.” For openKylin 3.0, the question is whether an open Linux desktop can transform AI from a separate application into a coordinated system capability—and do so with useful performance and meaningful human control.

PyTorch is at the heart of AI development, and increasingly the software layer through which hardware vendors compete for AI workloads.

SAN JOSE, Calif. — At the PyTorch Conference , the Big AI movers and shakers discussed the current state of PyTorch. And, well, they should since, as Amazon pointed out, “ 85% of AI researchers and developers write their code in PyTorch .”

### The New PyTorch Chips

At this week’s conference, the biggest news was that Google’s new TorchTPU backend and Amazon’s TorchNeuron both now support PyTorch to port existing PyTorch workloads to their accelerators. TorchTPU brings native PyTorch execution to Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), while TorchNeuron does essentially the same thing with Amazon’s AWS Trainium chips.

This is more than just supporting new chips with a familiar application programming interface (API). It also demands compilers, kernels, and distributed-training tools that can withstand expensive, long-running workloads.

As Chris Lattner, Qualcomm’s Executive VP of AI, said in his keynote, “We all know that PyTorch has done an amazing job at unifying the modeling layer, making it easy to build and train models for a wide variety of different applications, but we still have the bottom part of the stack that the hardware vendors have to make for themselves. This includes the kernels, the compilers, and low-level system software.”

That gap between a common modeling interface and fragmented execution infrastructure is becoming a central battleground in AI. Lattner added that creating a common framework is Qualcomm’s goal with the Modular software stack . Lattner described it as “something that’s like LLVM , [a collection of modular and reusable compiler and toolchain technologies for Linux] but for AI chips, and that’s what we’ve been building at Modular.”

He added Modular’s stack supports hardware from NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm, Amazon and Google. Making PyTorch as reusable as the framework above it on all chips is still a work in progress.

### Success Is Pressuring PyTorch’s Maintainers

PyTorch co-maintainer Alban Desmaison told attendees that more than 600,000 GitHub projects build on PyTorch and that the project receives roughly 150 pull requests daily. As a result, he said growing usage is straining testing, infrastructure, and release operations.

That’s a lot by any reckoning. PyTorch is growing to meet the demand. Mark Collier, the PyTorch Foundation executive director, reported that active contributors had increased 60% year over year, participating organizations 30% and pull requests 40%.

Desmaison also described shared hardware abstractions, backend integration and validation as essential framework responsibilities.

### PyTorch in Practice

PyTorch co-maintainer Edward Yang said closer work with large language model (LLM) training teams had reshaped his view of framework priorities. “At the end of the day, what you care about is how long it takes for you to get the final checkpoint that you’re actually going to serve.”

Peak utilization matters, but so do crashes, numerical errors, and code that engineers can understand and repair. Yang added users want codebases that let them resolve problems themselves when something goes wrong on the critical path.

His presentation emphasized the need to test large distributed workloads with fewer resources, improve profiling, and develop smaller, composable building blocks. We shouldn’t be, he continued, imposing an all-encompassing training system. Yang explained, “It’s impossible for us to anticipate any given problem any given user might have, so we want to build building blocks that you can easily adapt to your circumstances.”

Yang also previewed a lower-overhead profiler intended to remain enabled throughout training. He explicitly said it wasn’t publicly available yet.

### Shopify Shows What PyTorch Can Do in Business.

Shopify offered a concrete example of PyTorch’s role beyond frontier-model development: repeatedly improving a model for a narrowly defined business task.

Cody Mazza-Anthony, a Shopify Machine Learning (ML) engineer, described how the company provides its a ll-in-one cloud e-commerce platform used PyTorch to create a continual-learning workflow. It begins with a trusted ground-truth dataset and a model-based evaluator calibrated against human judgments. Once a system reaches production, Shopify identifies failures, repairs examples, adds successful corrections to its training data, and trains another model checkpoint.

In its buyer-profile application, the system converts shopping activity into structured representations of customers’ tastes and interests. Mazza-Anthony said Shopify began with approximately 29,000 examples and improved the specialized model through that production-feedback loop.

“It’s important to keep in mind that human agreement is the ceiling,” he said. “We’re not looking for perfect here. We’re looking for as good as human.”

Shopify’s presentation also described compressing system prompts into learned representations to reduce inference overhead. Together, the techniques show how businesses can use an open software stack to optimize task quality, latency and cost rather than continually substitute a larger general-purpose model.

### An Open Framework Is Not Open Source.

Meta’s presentation reinforced the view that PyTorch is becoming a collection of interoperable components spanning training, inference and optimization. Jana van Greunen, Meta’s Director of PyTorch Engineering, called Meta’s recently released Muse Spark Open models “open source models.” It’s not.

Its Muse Model License imposes usage restrictions and requires a separate agreement for qualifying model-as-a-service businesses above a $20-million revenue threshold. Those terms conflict with the Open Source Initiative’s (OSI) requirement that an open-source AI system be usable for any purpose without seeking permission.

That said, Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model .

### Openness Is AI’s Future.

Earlier, Collier had argued that open is the right way forward for both AI and PyTorch. He observed a DeepSeek model reportedly matched capability at 60% lower cost after 37 days; At the same time, NVIDIA work increased LLM inference performance by 68% on the same hardware in 33 days. This was all, he claimed, because they’d embraced the open approach.

He added, “co mpany after company and individuals from those companies that are really committed to working in the open, and that starts with open weights.” You can see the proof yourself. “PyTorch trains most of the models that we use every day,” and 70% of the new models use open weights. Other studies have shown that in just a few months, 56% of models processing AI Gateway tokens are open-weight models.

The moral of the story is that the future of AI is open, and PyTorch, itself an open-source language, is leading the way.
